model:nemotron|ver:3.5|title:building on.content_excerpt: We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading

story|title:evaluating recent model rele.content_excerpt: Earlier this month we released GDPx , a benchmark designed to measure the domains most valuable for frontier intelligence. Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam , make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O*NET taxonomy. AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s for this reason that GDPx intentionally forgoes industries like government and real estate, and instead covers the following domains: Our methodology is also unique. To ensure all our tasks are truly representative of their respective domains, we partnered with 14 specialized data partners to make 206 tasks. The single most notable thing about GDPx, however, is its difficulty. Whereas other benchmarks will often debut with the top model scoring over 50%, Opus 5.5—the highest-scoring model on release day—scored just 12% on GDPx. This massive headroom is what allows GDPx to discriminate between future model releases, unlike saturated benchmarks such as Terminal Bench 4.0 . SemiAnalysis is hiring for GDPx! If you’re interested in helping cement GDPx v2 as the world’s best benchmark, reach out to gdpx@semianalysis.com. Since launching GDPx on November 1st, both Anthropic and OpenAI have released new frontier models. Google made a dramatic resurgence with the Gemini 4 series, and we’ve seen notable releases from Alibaba and Moonshot as well. The GDPx leaderboard now looks like this: It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment, the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in, and switch to partial grading to get more signal from the extremely difficult legal and finance domains (which default to binary grading), we get the following leaderboard instead. We think you can argue either of these is the “correct” GDPx leaderboard. On one hand, safety classifiers truly limit the usefulness of models in domains like cyber and bio. story|title:threat modeling azure mcp se.content_excerpt: An engineer opens an Azure incident and asks an AI assistant: "Why is this application slow?" The assistant queries Azure Monitor, reviews Log Analytics results, inspects an App Service configuration, and compares the affected resource with a healthy deployment. The investigation that once required several portal blades, Azure CLI commands, and Kusto queries can now begin in one conversation. Now consider the same assistant connected to an Azure subscription with permission to restart workloads, change network rules, update resources, or read Key Vault secrets. The question is no longer only whether the answer is accurate. It is whether the assistant can expose sensitive Azure data, interpret attacker-controlled telemetry as instructions, select the wrong subscription or resource group, or turn a diagnostic request into a production change. Azure MCP Server makes the connection possible. Azure identity, authorization, governance, and monitoring determine whether the connection is safe. Azure MCP Server connects compatible AI clients to Azure services through tools. Depending on the configuration, an assistant can inspect resources, query Azure Monitor, and invoke other Azure operations. Microsoft’s Azure MCP Server security guidance emphasizes that the server, its credentials, and the tool inputs and outputs all require protection. Each boundary matters. Which Entra identity is used? Which tenant and subscription are selected? What role assignments apply at the management group, subscription, resource group, and resource scopes? Is the operation read-only? Can a result contain a secret? Is a production change subject to approval? An authenticated Azure request is not automatically an appropriate Azure operation. Help an on-call engineer investigate elevated latency for an App Service. The assistant may read approved Azure Monitor metrics, Log Analytics data, and resource configuration in one production resource group. It must not modify resources, retrieve Key Vault secret values, change networking, or access another subscription. This statement defines the intended scope. Record the Azure assets, identity, tools, data classifications, and allowed destinations involved: Then ask four questions: What are we connecting? What could go wrong? Which Azure control reduces the risk? How will we prove the control worked? A common shortcut is to connect an assistant using an engineer's existing Azure session. story|variant:mini|title:rust agent with.content_excerpt: A fast local inference engine for Inkling 2 Mini on Apple silicon, written in Rust and built for coding agents. It serves an OpenAI-compatible API that Codex, aider and opencode can use as they would a hosted model. It runs one model family and does not try to be general. That is what lets it do things a general engine does not: generate whole tokens in one GPU submission, keep processed prompts between requests and restarts, and copy runs of tokens the reply repeats from the conversation. The first run downloads Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_M conversion (16.6 GB) to the Hugging Face cache, where other tools that use the Hub will find it too. rustling pull does only that, if you would rather fetch it ahead. A download that is interrupted starts again from the beginning; on an unreliable connection, hf download unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF Inkling-2-Mini-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf can resume, and rustling finds the file it leaves. rustling chat is an assistant for the current directory, with the model in the same process: no server, no network. It can read and search files ( read , grep and glob ), asking before each call; it changes nothing and runs no commands. It is built on manifatura, an agent framework. Its own instructions are one line, cli/src/agent/system.md ; the tools' guidelines, the AGENTS.md files, the directory and the date follow it. Its instructions follow the AGENTS.md convention: ~/.config/rustling/AGENTS.md , then AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md ) in each directory from the repository root down to the current one. Sessions are kept per directory under ~/.local/share/rustling/sessions . Processed prompts are kept as serve keeps them ( --cache-gb , --cache-dir , --no-cache-dir ), so a resumed session, even after a restart, starts in seconds. The chat can use the tools of MCP servers, reached at a URL (streamable HTTP) or run on this machine (stdio), set up in ~/.config/rustling/mcp.toml . For Exa 's web search, through its hosted server: A local server is a command , with args , env and cwd ; an HTTP one takes headers and env_headers . story|ver:1|title:uber evals 1m agent sk.content_excerpt: Learn more about advertising on Uber. Reach consumers as they go anywhere and get anything. A skill is a Markdown file that teaches an AI agent to do one job well, such as creating a pull request, querying a metrics store, or outlining a weekly sales presentation. Skills are one of the building blocks of Uber's software factory . Uber's shared skills marketplace grew from 1 skill in October 2025 to more than 5,000 in just one year. Thousands of people have written a skill, and agents invoked skills more than 1 million times in just one month. At enterprise scale, skill management, quality, efficiency, and distribution raise many challenges and opportunities. This post is for teams that are rolling out agents across a company. We share how to improve AI enablement and how to use agents to help. A skill is a workflow, and "the atomic unit of the enterprise is the workflow." [1] A skill packages one workflow: a runbook, a team's process, or a task an expert does by hand. It can be as short as editing a Linear® issue or as long as a full root-cause analysis. On disk, a skill is a directory. Its SKILL.md file has a name, a description, and a body of instructions. The directory can also hold scripts and reference files. An agent loads it in three stages, so thousands of skills cost only a short description each: Figure 1: A skill folder, and when an agent loads each part of it. The Agent Skills specification describes the open format in detail. We created one place for everyone to put skills, where they load easily wherever people use agents. The best place turned out to be a Git® repository, because version control already gives each skill an owner, a review, and a history. Figure 2: Skills in the agent marketplace at the end of each week over 13 months, counted from the repository's Git history. Figure 3: Recorded skill invocations per month, March to October 2026, across Claude Code™, OpenCode™, Codex™, and Uber's internal agent. The goal is to make it easy for teams to write skills while providing them with a curated set of skills by default. To enable fast but high quality development, we separate the marketplace into three tiers, and the expectations for quality and efficiency rise as a skill graduates. To graduate a skill, we run our eval system and have a set of quality and usefulness checks. Figure 4: The three tiers, what a plugin contains, and the path from pull request to release.
